posts.caption: C7.10 one-page: the five paths, when each signal appears, and the day-75 decision
posts.comment:
Asked: define how a pilot becomes recurring revenue. Each path needs a trigger and a timing within the pilot, the negative signals have to be defined too, and the pricing has to come from C2.3.
Delivered: five paths, six negative signals, and an honest answer on price.

Takeaway: the earliest and most reliable expansion signal arrives at day 45, and it is the one most often missed. It is somebody OUTSIDE the pilot cohort asking for access. That is a demand signal rather than a results signal, so it shows up long before any outcome data exists, and it usually arrives looking like a nuisance request rather than like money. If it has not happened by day 45 it is not late, it simply has not happened, and the enterprise-license path should come out of the forecast.

Three of the five paths price cleanly from C2.3. Two do not, and the document says so rather than guessing. C2.3 covers staffed cohorts at $44,500 an engagement and self-paced licenses at $150 a learner a year in blocks of 60. Consulting and partner deployment sit outside both families and have no approved rate. A plausible number beside either of them is exactly how a deal gets priced in the room, which is the failure the C7.2 proposal template exists to prevent.

The consulting path is the dangerous one. It triggers around day 30, when the first real problem surfaces in a learner project and somebody realizes we could simply build it. It is the easiest revenue on the list and it is the path that turns this into a services firm, which is the precise thing the pilot hypothesis says we are trying not to be.

posts.caption: C7.10 the full framework: every path, the negative signals, and what C2.3 does not cover
posts.comment:
The full document: each path with its trigger, the reasoning behind that specific trigger, the signal day and the offer day, the price and its source, and the conversation owner. Then the six signals that say a customer will not expand, each with what to do rather than only what it means.

Read the first box before the rest. Colaberry has never run a pilot. C9.7, First Paid Lighthouse Customer, is still open. Every trigger and timing here is designed from the economics and from how these conversations usually go, not derived from a pilot we have run. The framework says so on both artifacts, because a document like this that reads as though it came from experience would be a lie told by register rather than by claim. The first real pilot tests this framework as much as it tests the delivery.

The negative signals are the half the ticket warned about. It names the failure mode directly: assuming expansion. The sharpest one is that the champion changes role, which is the most common cause of a dead renewal and has nothing to do with the quality of the work. The one that is ours rather than theirs is learners not producing verified evidence by day 60, because without verified work there is nothing to show at day 75 and the expansion conversation has no content at all.

Three things this framework deliberately does not claim. No conversion rate, because with zero pilots run there is no honest basis for one and a made-up rate would propagate into every forecast that cites it. No price for consulting or partner deployment. And the two floors referenced in C2.3 are named but not reproduced, because this document could not read their values; check them before discounting anything.
